full_judgment:
3. Mr Md Salahuddin Ahmed with Mr Md Ramzan Ali Sikder, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the Court while rejecting the application in not granting an order of ad-interim attachment caused irreparable loss and injury to the plaintiff-petitioner, if the scheduled property in respect of which attachment was sought, is removed from the jurisdiction of the learned Court it would obstruct and delay execution of the decree that may be obtained by the plaintiff petitioner and thus the leaned Court below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He has further submitted that the defendant-opposite parties have no assets in Bangladesh other than property described in the schedule herein below to satisfy the decree and if the scheduled property is removed from the jurisdiction of the learned Court below the purpose of filing of the application as well as the suit would be infructuous, thus the Court below arrived at a wrong decision in rejecting the application. Therefore, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. Lastly, he has submitted that the Court below while rejecting the application did not even consider the intention of the plaintiff as after long delay the opposite party is submitting the bank guarantee thus the Court below committed error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 4. Mr M Hafizullah along with Mr Md Ohiullah, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1-3 by filing affidavit-in-opposition, submits that the Court below has rightly refused to pass an order of attachment of the vessel before judgment directly. It is further submitted that there can be no order of attachment against the vessel 'MV Dusita Naree' under Order XXXVIII rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure inasmuch as there is nothing to show that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 had any intention to obstruct or delay the execution of an eventual decree. He has further submitted that a foreign ocean going vessel plies on international voyage from port to port in her ordinary course of business and 'MV Dusita Naree' came to Chittagong for discharge of cargo and after completion of the discharge of the cargo she was scheduled to sail for another international port in her ordinary course of business and, as such, 'MV Dusita Naree' was not liable to be attached under Order XXXVIII rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He has further submitted by referring decisions of this Court including the Appellate Division that under Order XXXVIII rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure movable properties usually brought within the Court's jurisdiction should not ordinarily be attached and a foreign ship which is calling at an international port on her usual voyage if comes within the jurisdiction of the court is not liable to be attached. Moreover, no property can be attached before judgment under the provisions of Order XXXVIII rule 5 on vague and general allegations made by the petitioner. Therefore, he prays that the bank guarantee be returned to the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-3. 

 5. The petitioner also filed an affidavit-in-reply against the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the defendant Nos. 1-3 that the petitioner reiterates the fact that in any type of commercial transactions, it is an implied condition that the carrier is under an obligation to use its knowledge and skill to ensure that the goods arrive at its destination in a good and sound condition and in same quantity as contracted for which the defendants failed to comply with. The Court below failed to appreciate the fact and further he has stated that the defendant No. 1 is the owner of the Vessel 'MV Dusita Naree' which is the only property of the defendant No. 1 in Bangladesh and if the vessel 'MV Dusita Naree' is allowed to leave the territorial jurisdiction of Bangladesh it will not only obstruct and delay the execution of the decree but also there would be left no property to satisfy the decree and, as such, the Court should make an order of attachment before judgment and prays for making the Rule absolute. 

 6. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, we have gone through the impugned judgment and order as well as the application made under Order XXXVIII rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the plaintiff. The suit is for realisation of the money as the plaintiffs suffer losses and the defendants have some liabilities to settle the issue with the plaintiff and there is a suit pending for determination of the claim. The petitioner apprehends that unless and until the order of attachment of vessel 'MV Dusita Naree' before judgment is passed the defendant-opposite parties may dispose of the said vessel and it will then go beyond the jurisdiction of the Court and it will obstruct the decree passed in the suit against them. The decision reported in 45 DLR 591 is as follows: 

 In another decision of the Appellate Division reported in 31 DLR (AD) 112 it has been held that unless and until an ad-interim attachment before judgment or bank guarantee is submitted the defendants have no other properties left in Bangladesh for adjudication to satisfy the decree in case succeed. In this connection we can refer 45 DLR 591 that the parties may resolve by taking recourse to an appropriate forum which is recognised in private International Law and to meet such situation remedy does not lie under Order XXXVIII rule 5 CPC and that has been supported in a case reported in 28 DLR 231. Further it appears from the un-reported case in Civil Petition No. 200 of 1990 wherein Transcontinental Imex Inc is the petitioner vs Formentors Maritime Inc and others respondents and it has been held that the bank guarantee was released by the High Court Division and that has been affirmed by the Appellate Division as there was nothing to show that the defendant had any intention to obstruct or delay the execution of the decree. Considering the cases reported in 28 DLR 231, 31 DLR (AD) 112 and 4 BCR 153, we do not find any reason to interfere in the order passed by the trial Court and the bank guarantee given in Court has no manner of application in this particular case. Nothing was shown as to whether there is any obstruction or delay in execution of eventual decree.
